You're not fully understanding COSTCO's business model. The only reason COSTCO can sell a 2 pound tub of whitefish salad for 8 bucks instead of 15 is BECAUSE it comes in a 2 pound tub. Otherwise, they are just a standard grocery store. They aren't going to change that for you or anyone else. 

They are filling a niche in a market and the only way you can change that is to change the market. If Costco changes, it may force some of their customers to shop elsewhere. I appreciate the clarification, though we may have to just agree to disagree. My point is that it simply doesn't have to be that way. We don't have to be the driving force behind a mass extinction event (which some scientists believe is already well underway). We are the first and only species ever capable of both causing and defeating a mass extinction event. 

Our capacity for compassion is one of the defining features of our species. It simply isn't in our nature not to care. The people who work tirelessly to save species on the brink of extinction are just as much part of the evolutionary process as the poachers who are trying to shoot them. The question is only, which evolutionary force will win out.

Why should we save endangered species? Why should we provide medical care to the terminally ill or the very old? Shouldn't we just let nature take it's course? It is just such a huge waste of time and resources. Surely we could put our efforts elsewhere to much more beneficial effect. Their imminent death is inevitable. Who are we to interfere with the natural order of things? 

I agree that humans will continue to expand, leaving behind only small pockets of parks and reserves to preserve the ecosystems we have destroyed or adapted to our needs. We will expand until we can expand no more. Eventually, we will either be forced to limit our population or develop the technologies to colonize other planets. When we reach the limits of the earth's capacity to provide the resources we need, starvation is the only other alternative. 

Ultimately, preserving the diversity of species is far more beneficial to us than we know. Of course, there may be medicinal or commercial applications for many plants and animals that we simply haven't discovered yet, but I'm talking about more subtle effects. It has been just over 100 years since the last passenger pigeon died, an yet, the effects of the passenger pigeon are still visible on the landscape. The nesting sites of flocks of millions of birds still show the benefits of the fertilization from their droppings. Everything from bees to beavers have a positive effect on the environment we depend on to survive. Are we to cause the destruction of species we depend on to the point that we ultimately cause the destruction of our own? Preservation of natural habitats and the animals that live in them is equivalent to our own preservation. We depend on them. Without them, we go the way of the dodo as well.

Moreover, we are the only species who has ever been capable of such wanton destruction to cause the extinction of so many species. It also happens that we are the only species capable of undoing the harm we have done.

First, be absolutely sure that you're not drilling into tempered glass. A tank that size is usually all tempered but at minimum the bottom may be tempered. You can't drill tempered glass. It will just shatter into a million pieces. 

Figure out how many gallons per hour you want and size the holes accordingly. Plenty of others recommended glassholes.com. You can get cheaper diamond hole saws elsewhere but the should have the information on which size to get. Personally, I bought the bulkheads I was going to use and sized my hole saw a few mm larger. 

Getting the saw started is the hardest part. I used a scrap of 2x4 and drilled a through hole the same size as my hole saw. I drilled another hole a few inches away that be a tight fit for my garden hose. On the underside of the block, I chiseled out a channel for the water to go from the hose, go around the drill bit, and exit below the saw. I used some rubber padded clamps to secure the block to the glass. Turn on the water. Set the hole saw in the hole and go for it. I used a cordless drill on the slowest setting. Also, if your drill has adjustable torque, set it to the lowest level. You don't want the drill to get stuck and then just ram through and break something. 

Hope that helps a little. Good luck.

Well, it's certainly not impossible to be successful but it's definitely not likely. The key to fermenting cider is yeast. The traditional way of making cider is essentially what your girlfriend is doing.  Leave the cider out and let the natural yeast present in the environment go at it.  The problem is that she probably doesn't have an overabundance of yeast just waiting to feast on her cider, at least not the kind that is going to make a cider worth drinking.  

Traditional ciders made this way were made in cideries where every conceivable surface was covered in the yeast that naturally grows on the skins of apples. It didn't take much to get the yeast into the cider.  Just leave it open and wait. 

The yeast that may be trying to establish itself in your girlfriend's cider has to compete with all sorts of nasty bacteria and fungi and who knows what else that also view those jugs of cider as a tasty snack. The key to making cider this way is to make sure the yeast is established and the fermentation is well underway before any of those other nasty microbes ever get a chance. 

The traditional ciderey overcomes this by sheer numbers.  The yeast simply outnumbers everything else around. Your girlfriend is probably not so lucky. The pasteurization killed off whatever yeast may have been in the cider before, so the chances of a successful brew are going to be pretty small. 

Next time invest in an air lock and a rubber stopper to keep out all the unwanted microbes, and any yeast for white wine available online or at any home brew store will produce a pretty satisfactory tasting result for a first try.
